q: What is a Monte Carlo method in RL?
short: A method that estimates values by averaging returns from complete sampled episodes, with no model of the environment and no bootstrapping.
detail: Works for episodic tasks; updates at episode end.

q: First-visit vs every-visit MC?
short: First-visit averages the return following the first occurrence of a state in each episode; every-visit uses all occurrences. Both converge to v_π.
example: A state visited twice in one episode.

q: Compute V(C) and V(E) in the five-state example.
follow: What would DP say V(E) is?

q: Why must MC control estimate Q rather than V?
short: Without a model you cannot do one-step lookahead from V to pick an action; Q(s, a) ranks actions directly.

q: What are exploring starts?
short: An assumption that each episode starts from a random state–action pair with every pair having non-zero probability, guaranteeing all Q(s, a) get samples.
detail: Realistic in simulation, not in the real world.

q: Define an ε-soft policy and the ε-greedy probabilities.
short: π(a|s) ≥ ε/|A| for every action. ε-greedy: greedy action 1 − ε + ε/|A|, each other action ε/|A|.

q: On-policy vs off-policy learning?
short: On-policy evaluates/improves the policy that generates the data; off-policy learns about a target policy π from data generated by a behaviour policy b, requiring coverage and usually importance sampling.

q: List strengths and weaknesses of direct MC evaluation.
short: Strengths: simple, model-free, unbiased, independent of other estimates, robust to non-Markov states. Weaknesses: needs complete episodes, high variance, ignores transition structure, sample-hungry.

q: Explain why V(B) = 8 and V(E) = −2 although both go to C.
short: MC treats each state's estimate independently using only episodes that visited it; E's sample included the −10 exit while B's didn't. With the model (or bootstrapping) both would be −1 + V(C).
detail: Sampling artefact; vanishes with infinite data.

q: Why does ε-soft control converge only to the best ε-soft policy?
short: Improvement is restricted to ε-soft policies (they must keep probability ε/|A| on every action), so the fixed point is optimal within that class, slightly worse than the deterministic optimum.
detail: Policy improvement theorem within the class.

q: Why do transition probabilities cancel in the importance ratio?
short: Trajectory probability under π is Π π(Aₖ|Sₖ)p(Sₖ₊₁|Sₖ, Aₖ) and under b the same with b; the p terms appear in both and cancel, leaving Π π/b.
follow: What if π and b are deterministic and differ?

q: Ordinary vs weighted importance sampling?
short: OIS divides weighted returns by the count: unbiased, variance possibly infinite. WIS divides by the sum of weights: biased (→ 0 with data), bounded/low variance; preferred.
detail: With one sample WIS returns G itself.

q: Why is blackjack a good MC example?
short: The model is complicated (dealer's sequential draws) but simulation is trivial; episodes are short and always terminate; γ = 1 makes return = final reward.

q: Incremental MC: returns 9, 9, −11, 9. Show the estimate after each.
example: Constant α would weight recent returns more.

q: Is MC robust to non-Markov states? Why?
short: More than TD: MC never uses one-step structure or other states' estimates, so a non-Markov state just gets the average return following it under the data distribution.

q: Design an off-policy evaluation of a new recommendation policy from logs.
short: Log propensities b(a|s); compute per-session ratios π/b; use weighted IS (or doubly robust with a reward model); clip extreme weights; check effective sample size and coverage; report confidence intervals.
example: New policy recommends items never shown before → no coverage.

q: Why does off-policy MC control learn slowly?
short: With a greedy target, it can only learn from the tail of each episode after the last non-greedy behaviour action; exploratory actions early in long episodes cut learning to a few final steps.

q: MC prediction cost per state compared with DP?
short: MC cost to estimate one state doesn't depend on the number of states (sample episodes from it), whereas DP sweeps all states. Useful when only a few states' values matter.
detail: Basis of rollout and MCTS evaluation.
mistakes: Assuming MC must estimate every state.

q: When should you use constant-α MC?
short: In nonstationary settings (changing environment or policy during control), so older returns from earlier policies are forgotten; also typical with function approximation (gradient MC).
example: MC control where the policy keeps changing.

q: How does the blackjack MC run illustrate estimation noise?
short: After 400k hands most cells match basic strategy, but boundary cells (e.g. 16 vs dealer 10) flip because the true Q-values for hit and stick are nearly equal and MC averages have standard error ~1/√N.
detail: Need more samples or decaying ε.
